<!-- Detailed Description - body text only, no heading line. -->

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the proportion of the underside of the covering element 36 that is wetted by the bonding material 40, and improves the contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38 throughout each vibration cycle. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside the contact rather than lying between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without downward force applied by an operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

# FIG. 5 - Second embodiment with a pulling element

- The vibration device 10 is a shallow rectangular assembly standing on the covering element 36, drawn as on FIG. 1: the base, drawn as a flat slab, a rectangular motor housing and a separate rectangular pump housing, both standing on the base and not touching each other, and a grip carried on the base, clear of those housings. Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator does not have to press the device against the covering element and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is removed rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base, the perimeter member and the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element without being absorbed on the way. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.
---
The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.
The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

content.text:
All twelve findings are fixed. Text changes were confined to the five sentences the review identified; the claims, numeral table and disclosed embodiments are unchanged.

**Text (draft/)**
- Summary: the comparative "coupled harder and held down harder than a pressed-on sliding base" is gone; the sentence now states only the disclosed proposition, no intervening compliant member or air film.
- Detailed description: the discrete "joint" and its transmission property become "rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16"; the transmission-path sentence now reads "into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16"; "rubber bush or foam pad" becomes the claim-matching "elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount"; "throughout each vibration cycle" deleted.
- Brief Description: FIG. 1 entry now says "shown in use on a covering element", matching that sheet's new numeral 36.

**Figures**
- Handle 44 is no longer one of a counted set of bodies on the first side; on FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 it is a grip carried on the base, standing clear of the two housings. The self-contradictory "one of three bodies / to the right of the three bodies" instruction is gone, and the motor is placed as "the left-hand of the two housings".
- Motor and pump: order and spacing along the slab removed; only their distinctness as separate, non-touching housings remains.
- FIG. 5: single tile as in FIG. 1, no multi-tile floor or joint lines; perimeter member 24 is now "the only part of the vibration device 10 that touches the covering element 36", which removes the conflict with the pulling element lying over the tile.
- FIG. 1 now labels covering element 36, giving it seven numerals, and base 12 targets a broad interior of its exposed top face instead of the narrow front band.
- Naming: "plate", "the tile" and bare "the loop" replaced by base, covering element and perimeter member 24, with slab/tile/column/band kept only as appositives. On FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 the parent parts are named without numerals, since 12 is not labelled on those sheets.

Verified after the edits: the same 16 numerals across the five sheets and the table, at most seven on any sheet, every brief between 1,606 and 2,592 characters, and no note, placeholder, question or em dash anywhere in `draft/` or `figures/`.

input.summary: Fixed all twelve review findings: two untraced statements in the filing text (the comparative holding-force result in the Summary and the discrete perimeter-to-base joint in the description), three smaller untraced description details, the undisclosed handle mounting and the self-contradictory body count on FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, the FIG. 5 contact conflict and multi-tile floor, the undisclosed motor-and-pump order and spacing, the missing numeral 36 on FIG. 1, the narrow base 12 target on FIG. 1, and the shape words that differed from numeral-table part names across FIG. 2, FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5. Claims, numeral table and disclosed embodiments are unchanged.
reasoning: The Summary's claim that the device is 'held down harder than a pressed-on sliding base' asserted a magnitude comparison the disclosure never makes. The inventor says the differential holds the device firmly without the operator pressing, which is sufficiency, not superiority over a pressed base. The sentence now records only what is disclosed: coupling without an intervening compliant member or air film, with the operator's hands carrying less. Nothing in the claims depended on the deleted comparison, so no claim moved.

The description twice treated the perimeter-to-base interface as a discrete joint with its own transmission property. The disclosure describes the perimeter as formed at the perimeter of the second side and is silent on how it is attached, and an earlier corrective message removed the converse detail of a one-piece loop, so neither formation is affirmatively supported. The text now says the perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, which is the general rigidity of the load path that the disclosure does support and which is what claim 1's all-rigid path limitation rests on.

The handle findings were the ones with the most potential to leak invention. Both perspective sheets had handle 44 standing on the first side as one of three bodies in a fixed left-to-right order, and FIG. 1 then placed that same body to the right of all three, which cannot be drawn. The disclosure says only that the device may include one or more handles used for guiding. Both briefs now show a grip carried on the base and standing clear of the two housings, with no stated position relative to motor or pump, and the motor is placed as the left-hand of the two housings rather than by a count that includes itself. I did not add a mounting location to the description to justify the old drawing; I removed it from the drawing instead.

The FIG. 5 conflict was real and unresolvable as written: the perimeter member cannot be the only body touching the tile while a slack line sags across the same tile. Since the pulling element is connected to the device but is not part of the device, the fix is to say perimeter member 24 is the only part of the vibration device 10 that touches the covering element 36. That keeps the disclosed relationship, the rigid rim being the sole contact of the machine, while letting the line lie where a rope must lie.

FIG. 5's floor of several tiles with joint lines was invented, and it also disagreed with FIG. 1's single tile. It mattered more than a stray detail because two numeral targets were built on those joint lines. The sheet now shows the covering element 36 as one large plain tile as in FIG. 1, numeral 36 targets its exposed surface clear of the device and clear of the pulling element, and the pulling element runs over the covering element 36 and off the sheet in one unbroken path with no joint-line crossing rule.

FIG. 1 showed the covering element and expressly denied it a numeral while the same part is numbered 36 on three other sheets. Adding 36 takes that sheet to seven numerals, inside the eight-per-sheet limit, and closes the mapping. I also synchronized the Brief Description of the Drawings so FIG. 1 is described as shown in use on a covering element, which is what the sheet now labels.

On naming, base 12 was travelling as 'plate', covering element 36 as 'the tile' and perimeter member 24 as 'the loop'. I moved every brief to the numeral-table name and kept slab, tile, column and band only as appositives introduced against the proper name. On FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 I used the bare table names base and covering element rather than base 12, because numeral 12 is not labelled on those sheets and putting the numeral in the prose would imply a label the sheet does not carry; on FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, where 12 is labelled, the numeral is used.

Two smaller description items were engineering inference rather than disclosure and are gone: contact maintained 'throughout each vibration cycle', which is a per-oscillation dynamic assertion the inventor never makes, and the negation of a 'rubber bush' and 'foam pad', which named structures the source never names. The motor-mount sentence now uses the same elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount wording as claim 1 and the transmission-path paragraph, so the negative limitation reads identically in all three places, which is what antecedent consistency needs if that limitation is ever argued.

Claim 1 is untouched and its distinguishing combination is intact: a rigid perimeter member ending in a low-friction bearing face with a clearance admitting ambient air continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber sub-atmospheric under that ingress, and an all-rigid motor-to-bearing-face path with the face slidable while the differential is maintained. None of the deleted text supported a claim limitation; the joint sentence in particular was narrower than the claim, which recites only that the perimeter member extends from the second side.

data.summary: Fixed all twelve review findings: two untraced statements in the filing text (the comparative holding-force result in the Summary and the discrete perimeter-to-base joint in the description), three smaller untraced description details, the undisclosed handle mounting and the self-contradictory body count on FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, the FIG. 5 contact conflict and multi-tile floor, the undisclosed motor-and-pump order and spacing, the missing numeral 36 on FIG. 1, the narrow base 12 target on FIG. 1, and the shape words that differed from numeral-table part names across FIG. 2, FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5. Claims, numeral table and disclosed embodiments are unchanged.
reasoning: The Summary's claim that the device is 'held down harder than a pressed-on sliding base' asserted a magnitude comparison the disclosure never makes. The inventor says the differential holds the device firmly without the operator pressing, which is sufficiency, not superiority over a pressed base. The sentence now records only what is disclosed: coupling without an intervening compliant member or air film, with the operator's hands carrying less. Nothing in the claims depended on the deleted comparison, so no claim moved.

The description twice treated the perimeter-to-base interface as a discrete joint with its own transmission property. The disclosure describes the perimeter as formed at the perimeter of the second side and is silent on how it is attached, and an earlier corrective message removed the converse detail of a one-piece loop, so neither formation is affirmatively supported. The text now says the perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, which is the general rigidity of the load path that the disclosure does support and which is what claim 1's all-rigid path limitation rests on.

The handle findings were the ones with the most potential to leak invention. Both perspective sheets had handle 44 standing on the first side as one of three bodies in a fixed left-to-right order, and FIG. 1 then placed that same body to the right of all three, which cannot be drawn. The disclosure says only that the device may include one or more handles used for guiding. Both briefs now show a grip carried on the base and standing clear of the two housings, with no stated position relative to motor or pump, and the motor is placed as the left-hand of the two housings rather than by a count that includes itself. I did not add a mounting location to the description to justify the old drawing; I removed it from the drawing instead.

The FIG. 5 conflict was real and unresolvable as written: the perimeter member cannot be the only body touching the tile while a slack line sags across the same tile. Since the pulling element is connected to the device but is not part of the device, the fix is to say perimeter member 24 is the only part of the vibration device 10 that touches the covering element 36. That keeps the disclosed relationship, the rigid rim being the sole contact of the machine, while letting the line lie where a rope must lie.

FIG. 5's floor of several tiles with joint lines was invented, and it also disagreed with FIG. 1's single tile. It mattered more than a stray detail because two numeral targets were built on those joint lines. The sheet now shows the covering element 36 as one large plain tile as in FIG. 1, numeral 36 targets its exposed surface clear of the device and clear of the pulling element, and the pulling element runs over the covering element 36 and off the sheet in one unbroken path with no joint-line crossing rule.

FIG. 1 showed the covering element and expressly denied it a numeral while the same part is numbered 36 on three other sheets. Adding 36 takes that sheet to seven numerals, inside the eight-per-sheet limit, and closes the mapping. I also synchronized the Brief Description of the Drawings so FIG. 1 is described as shown in use on a covering element, which is what the sheet now labels.

On naming, base 12 was travelling as 'plate', covering element 36 as 'the tile' and perimeter member 24 as 'the loop'. I moved every brief to the numeral-table name and kept slab, tile, column and band only as appositives introduced against the proper name. On FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 I used the bare table names base and covering element rather than base 12, because numeral 12 is not labelled on those sheets and putting the numeral in the prose would imply a label the sheet does not carry; on FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, where 12 is labelled, the numeral is used.

Two smaller description items were engineering inference rather than disclosure and are gone: contact maintained 'throughout each vibration cycle', which is a per-oscillation dynamic assertion the inventor never makes, and the negation of a 'rubber bush' and 'foam pad', which named structures the source never names. The motor-mount sentence now uses the same elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount wording as claim 1 and the transmission-path paragraph, so the negative limitation reads identically in all three places, which is what antecedent consistency needs if that limitation is ever argued.

Claim 1 is untouched and its distinguishing combination is intact: a rigid perimeter member ending in a low-friction bearing face with a clearance admitting ambient air continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber sub-atmospheric under that ingress, and an all-rigid motor-to-bearing-face path with the face slidable while the differential is maintained. None of the deleted text supported a claim limitation; the joint sentence in particular was narrower than the claim, which recites only that the perimeter member extends from the second side.

-The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside the contact rather than lying between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

+The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside the contact rather than lying between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside that contact, being present only along part of the perimeter member 24 rather than separating the bearing face 26 from the exposed face 38 everywhere: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.
=== FIG5 ===
The covering element 36, drawn as one large plain tile as in FIG. 1, fills the lower part of the sheet and is otherwise plain. A machine stands on it, and the surface of the covering element 36 is exposed around the machine.

- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile, on which the vibration device 10 stands. Identified well inside the exposed surface of that tile, clear of the vibration device 10 and clear of the flexible pulling element 46.
- The vibration device 10 is a shallow rectangular assembly standing on the covering element 36, drawn as on FIG. 1: the base, drawn as a flat slab, a rectangular motor housing and a separate rectangular pump housing, both standing on the base and not touching each other, and a grip carried on the assembly, clear of those housings. The whole assembly is drawn with one continuous outer silhouette. Identified on that continuous outer silhouette.
- The perimeter member 24 is a shallow rectangular band standing under the base and running round its underside at its edge, so the base is held clear of the covering element 36 by that band; its outward-facing front surface is visible below the base, and it is the only part of the vibration device 10 that touches the covering element 36. Identified well inside that visible front surface.
- The handle 44 is that grip, standing clear of the two housings. Identified well inside its outline.
- The flexible pulling element 46 is the one slack flexible line on the sheet, drawn as a single curved path of even thickness and the only curving element on the sheet. The line meets the vibration device 10 at its outer silhouette and runs away from it over the covering element 36, sagging gently, and runs off the edge of the sheet in one unbroken path, without doubling back or crossing itself. Identified on that curved line where it runs over the covering element 36 clear of the vibration device 10.

All five findings are fixed, with changes confined to the sentences the review identified.

**Figures**
- FIG. 5: the pulling element now meets the vibration device 10 at its outer silhouette rather than at the base, so no attachment point is fixed; the grip is "carried on the assembly".
- FIG. 1: the handle is "a grip carried on the vibration device 10", which also removes the mismatch with line 7 of the same brief ("carried on the machine").

**Text**
- Detailed description, clearance paragraph: the contrast with a prior-art air film is now stated as extent rather than location. It reads "does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop" and "being present only along part of the perimeter member 24 rather than separating the bearing face 26 from the exposed face 38 everywhere", matching the "along at least part of the perimeter member" language of line 37 and of claims 1, 10 and 14.
- Brief Description of FIG. 4: now "of the lower end of the perimeter member and the covering element beneath it, taken at a place along the perimeter member where the clearance is present", which agrees with the FIG. 4 geometry in which the column stands above the covering element.
- Handle cross-reference: the Handles paragraph now reads "one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5", and the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 entries in the Brief Description each note the device carrying a handle. The FIG. 5 entry also now says the pulling element is "connected to" the device, tracking the disclosure's own word.

Claims, numeral table and disclosed embodiments are unchanged. Re-verified: the same 16 numerals across table, description and sheets, at most seven per sheet, briefs between 1,606 and 2,592 characters, and no note, placeholder, question or em dash in `draft/` or `figures/`.

input.summary: Fixed all five findings: the untraced attachment of pulling element 46 at the base and the untraced mounting of handle 44 on the base are removed from the figure briefs, the clearance paragraph no longer denies the location that claim 1 recites, the Brief Description of FIG. 4 no longer states contact where the sheet shows the clearance, and handle 44 is now tied to FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 in both the detailed description and the drawing descriptions. Claims, numeral table and disclosed embodiments are unchanged.
reasoning: The two critical findings were the same class of defect: a figure brief fixing a structural relationship the inventor never states. The disclosure says the pulling element is connected to the device and that the device may include one or more handles, and stops there. Both briefs had gone further, joining the line to the base and carrying the grip on the base. The line now meets the vibration device 10 at its outer silhouette and the grip is carried on the vibration device 10 or on the assembly, so each sheet shows the connection the disclosure supports without asserting where on the machine it lands. I fixed this in the drawing rather than by adding a mounting location to the description, because the description is not allowed to grow to justify a sheet.

The FIG. 1 handle fix also cured an internal inconsistency inside that one brief, where line 7 said the grip is carried on the machine and the bullet said carried on the base 12. Both now say the same thing.

The clearance paragraph was the finding with real prosecution consequences. Claim 1, claim 10 and claim 14 all recite the clearance as remaining between the bearing face and the exposed face along at least part of the perimeter member, and line 37 of the description says the same. The later paragraph then denied that the clearance lies between those faces, which reads as a written-description denial of the claim limitation. The distinction the paragraph was actually drawing is extent, not location: a prior-art air film separates the whole area, whereas this clearance exists only along part of the loop. Rewriting it as 'does not separate ... over the whole of the loop' and 'being present only along part of the perimeter member 24 rather than separating ... everywhere' keeps the argument that the contact, not the clearance, carries the vibration, while using the same relationship for the same recited element as the claims.

The FIG. 4 finding was a straight contradiction between the filed drawing description and the depicted geometry. The sheet is expressly taken where the clearance is present, so the column stands above the covering element and the two nowhere touch; saying the perimeter member end meets the covering element there described a contact the sheet excludes. The entry now describes the lower end of the perimeter member and the covering element beneath it, taken at a place along the perimeter member where the clearance is present, which matches both the brief and the description paragraph that explains why FIG. 2 shows no gap at its scale and FIG. 4 shows the gap enlarged.

For the handle cross-reference I did the prescribed fix and one step more. The description paragraph now says the handles are shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, and the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 entries in the Brief Description each mention the device carrying a handle, because the finding noted that neither entry did. I left the overview paragraph listing what the device comprises alone: the handle is optional in the disclosure and in claim 8, so it does not belong in the comprises sentence.

While in the FIG. 5 entry I changed 'attached to the device' to 'connected to the device', which is the disclosure's own word for the pulling element and avoids implying an attachment formation, the very detail an earlier corrective message listed as unsupported.

Nothing in the claims moved. The clearance limitation, the all-rigid transmission path, the slidable bearing face and the decoupled-control system claim are as filed, and the sixteen numeral definitions are untouched. The edits removed unsupported figure structure and aligned description wording to the claims rather than the reverse.

input.prior_art_strategy: Claim 1 is unchanged and still clears the references on the same combination, and this turn's edit to the clearance paragraph strengthens rather than weakens the position. US-11408462-B2 holds its body down with partitions expressly formed of elastic members, with rigidity added only as a restricting frame to stop the elastomer being drawn into the decompression space, and US-4934475-A recites a seal member cooperating with the wall to define the pressure reduction space. Claim 1 recites the opposite design choice: a rigid perimeter member terminating in a low-friction bearing face, with a clearance remaining along at least part of it through which ambient air enters the chamber continuously, and an extraction rate sufficient to keep the chamber below atmospheric while that ingress continues. The description now states that relationship in the same words in every place it appears, so the paragraph explaining why the clearance is not a defect no longer reads as a denial of the claim's own location language; it explains instead that the clearance exists only along part of the loop while the rest of the loop makes hard contact, which is exactly the technical reason the arrangement couples better than a pressed-on sliding base separated over its whole area by an air film. No drafting note, placeholder, bracketed request, open question, or unresolved alternative remains in the patent text, and claim/description terminology is uniform. The disclosure never gives any dimension, magnitude, ratio, or order of size for the gap beneath the perimeter. It says only that the perimeter is not intended to seal and that it restricts airflow. "Restricts airflow" does not affirmatively establish any true height, nor that the true height is below drawable scale. There is no affirmative passage in the disclosure or in any USER turn stating a clearance dimension; the nearest source wording is the qualitative "it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile." The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

lines: Overview

-FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the proportion of the underside of the covering element 36 that is wetted by the bonding material 40, and improves the contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

lines: Method of use

-A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without downward force applied by an operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

<!-- Summary - body text only, no heading line. -->

A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and its bearing face is of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.

Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator does not have to press the device against the covering element and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is removed rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base, the perimeter member and the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element without being absorbed on the way. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.

Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.

In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.

A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.

<!-- Background - body text only, no heading line. -->

When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.

Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place.

Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.

The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.

What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.

Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base, the perimeter member and the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element without being absorbed on the way. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.

Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.

In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.

A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.

A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and its bearing face is of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.

A vibration device for bedding covering elements into thinset, mortar or adhesive has a rigid base carrying a vibration motor and an air-extraction mechanism on its first side and a chamber on its second side. A rigid perimeter member surrounds the chamber and ends in a bearing face of low-friction material such as plastic or PTFE. It is not a seal: a clearance remains against the exposed face of the covering element, and ambient air enters the chamber continuously. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air fast enough to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure while air keeps entering, and the pressure differential presses the device onto the covering element without downward force being required from the operator. Every member between the motor and the covering element is rigid, so vibration transfers with little damping, and the bearing face lets the device slide to successive areas without releasing the hold.

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

=== para 55 ===
53:The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

FIG. 1 is a perspective view of a vibration device according to a first embodiment, shown in use on a covering element and carrying a handle.

FIG. 2 is a vertical sectional view of the vibration device of FIG. 1 resting on a covering element, taken through the base, the chamber and the perimeter member, the vibration motor, the air-extraction mechanism and the handle being omitted for clarity, and the communication between the air-extraction mechanism and the chamber not being shown.

FIG. 3 is a bottom plan view of the vibration device of FIG. 1, showing the second side of the base and the perimeter member.

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary sectional view of the lower end of the perimeter member and the covering element beneath it, taken at a place along the perimeter member where the clearance is present, showing the bearing face at the lower end of the perimeter member, the clearance between the bearing face and the exposed face of the covering element, and the covering element bedded in bonding material spread over a substrate.

FIG. 5 is a perspective view of a second embodiment in which a flexible pulling element is connected to the device for drawing the device across a covering element.
A vibration device for bedding covering elements into thinset, mortar or adhesive has a rigid base carrying a vibration motor and an air-extraction mechanism on its first side and a chamber on its second side. A rigid perimeter member surrounds the chamber and ends in a bearing face of low-friction material such as plastic or PTFE. It is not a seal: a clearance remains against the exposed face of the covering element, and ambient air enters the chamber continuously. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air fast enough to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure while air keeps entering, and the pressure differential presses the device onto the covering element without downward force being required from the operator. Every member between the motor and the covering element is rigid, so vibration transfers with little damping, and the bearing face lets the device slide to successive areas without releasing the hold.
wherein a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passes through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

wherein the bearing face is slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained.
a vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber,

the perimeter member being rigid and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face of a low-friction material, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed in contact with an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber,

content.text:
All eleven findings are fixed.

**Description**
- Clearance magnitude: "far too small to be drawn to scale" and "many times its true height" replaced by "The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity", with FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 described as the reviewer prescribed.
- Clearance geometry: the exclusive partition of the interface is gone. The paragraph now says the bearing face bears rigidly on the exposed face and carries the vibration, and that the clearance, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits air without a compliant member separating the faces, matching the "along at least part" recital in claims 1, 10 and 14.
- Operator force: the absolutes are permissive throughout, including the method-of-use paragraph, which used the same phrasing.
- Loop shape: added that the rectangular plan outline is by way of example only and the perimeter member may follow any closed outline around the chamber.
- Effects sentence: wetting replaced by increased area of contact and a strengthened bond.
- Handles paragraph now points to FIG. 1 only.

**Claims**: claim 6 now ties continuous withdrawal to the device being in use, verbatim with the description; claim 17's absolute becomes "without a downward force being required from the operator", the model used in claims 5 and 13.

**Summary, Abstract, Brief Description**: operator wording aligned (abstract still 148 words); FIG. 2 entry now lists the handle among the parts omitted for clarity; the FIG. 5 entry no longer mentions a handle.

**Figures**: FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 recast the motor and pump as two simple housings carried on the base with no shapes, ordering, spacing or overhang asserted, and the base's top face is "visible where no body stands on it"; FIG. 2 drops "of even thickness"; FIG. 4 shows the gap as an open space so the clearance is visible, with "greatly enlarged" and "tall" removed; FIG. 5 no longer shows a handle, leaving numerals 10, 24, 36, 46. Handle 44 remains labelled on FIG. 1, so every numeral still appears on at least one sheet.

**numerals.md**: the process preamble is deleted, leaving the heading and the 16-row table. The `<!-- ... -->` template comments are removed from all nine section files.

input.summary: Fixed all eleven findings: the unsourced clearance magnitude and the exclusive clearance-here/contact-elsewhere geometry are out of the description, the absolute operator-force statements are permissive in the description, claim 17, the Summary and the Abstract, claim 6 now matches the description's continuous-extraction condition, the invented housing shapes, spacing, base overhang, even-thickness base and the handle on the pulling-element sheet are out of the briefs, the rectangular loop is now stated in the description as an example only, the FIG. 2 omission list and the wetting mechanism are corrected, and the process scaffolding is removed from numerals.md and from the nine section files.
reasoning: The clearance magnitude was the most dangerous item, because a stated dimensional fact about the gap is a limitation a reader can hold the application to and the inventor never gave any size. The description now says only that the clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity, which is a drawing convention rather than an assertion about the device, and the FIG. 4 brief no longer justifies its gap by the invented smallness of the real one; it asks for an open space sized so the clearance is visible. I also removed 'greatly' from the FIG. 4 view line and 'tall' from the bearing face bullet, since both carried the same unsourced premise.

The clearance geometry paragraph had drifted into asserting a partition of the interface: gap along part of the loop, hard contact over the remainder, vibration crossing at the contact and not at the gap. The disclosure affirms air entering beneath the perimeter and rigid contact with the tile, but not where each occurs. The paragraph now says the bearing face bears rigidly on the exposed face and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact, and that the clearance, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits air without a compliant member separating the faces. That keeps literal, in-the-same-words support for the 'along at least part of the perimeter member' recital in claims 1, 10 and 14 while dropping the exclusive version.

The operator-force item was both a fidelity and a scope defect, so I fixed it in every place it appeared rather than only the two cited. Claim 17 recited the absolute as a positive method limitation and now recites that the pressure differential holds the device without a downward force being required from the operator, which is the construction claims 5 and 13 already used. The description's 'hands carry no part of the contact load', 'the operator applies no downward force' and 'the only force the operator supplies' are now permissive, and I made the same correction in the method-of-use paragraph, which carried the identical phrasing and would otherwise have contradicted the amended claim.

For the invented figure geometry I recast structure as depiction convention rather than deleting the bodies. The motor and the air-extraction mechanism are now simply the two bodies carried on the top face of the base, each shown as a simple housing, with no rectangular shape, no left-or-right assignment, no non-touching requirement and no base overhang. The overhang mattered most because it existed to manufacture a labelling target; the base 12 endpoint is now 'well inside the visible part of its top face', which is a broad interior on the intended part and does not require the slab to run past anything.

On the handle in the pulling-element embodiment I took the narrower option the reviewer identified as source-safest: numeral 44 and the grip are gone from FIG. 5, the Brief Description no longer says the device again carries a handle, and the description points the handle to FIG. 1 alone. Handle 44 is still labelled on FIG. 1, so no numeral lost its sheet and no part or definition was deleted. The alternative would have required the specification to assert a both-at-once configuration the disclosure presents as separate embodiments.

Claim 6 recited a relationship neither the description nor the source states, tying continuous extraction to motor operation. It now reads 'continuously while the vibration device is in use', word for word with the description. This is a narrowing of nothing: the disclosure's continuity statement is about the device in use, and claim 1 already carries the extraction-rate limitation that does the work against the art.

The rectangular loop is a case where the drawings had to show some shape while the text was shape-neutral. I fixed it in the description, adding that the rectangular plan outline is shown by way of example only and that the perimeter member 24 may follow any closed outline around the chamber at the perimeter of the second side. That keeps claim 2's closed-loop recital broad rather than being read down to a rectangle, and it let the FIG. 3 geometry stand unchanged. I did remove the stray 'rectangular' from the perimeter band in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, where it added nothing.

Two small reconciliations: the FIG. 2 entry now lists the handle with the motor and the air-extraction mechanism as omitted for clarity, matching a brief that omits everything carried on the first side; and the overview sentence now says the vibration increases the area of contact between covering element 36 and bonding material 40 and strengthens the bond, which are the effects the disclosure lists, instead of a wetting mechanism it does not give.

The process scaffolding is gone from numerals.md, leaving the heading and the sixteen-row table, and I also stripped the template comment from the head of each of the nine section files rather than leaving them to a render step, since the standing rule is that no instruction may appear anywhere in draft/.

Nothing in claim 1, claim 10 or claim 14 changed. The distinguishing combination is untouched: a rigid perimeter member ending in a low-friction bearing face with a clearance along at least part of it admitting ambient air continuously, an extraction rate holding the chamber below atmospheric under that ingress, and an all-rigid motor-to-bearing-face path with the face slidable while the differential is maintained. The edits removed unsourced description gloss around those limitations and aligned two dependent claims to the description, which strengthens written-description support rather than narrowing scope.

input.prior_art_strategy: Claim 1, claim 10 and claim 14 are unchanged and clear the references on the same combination. US-11408462-B2 holds its body down with partitions expressly formed of elastic members, rigidity appearing only as a restricting frame that stops the elastomer being drawn into the decompression space, and US-4934475-A recites a seal member cooperating with the wall to define the pressure reduction space. Claim 1 recites the opposite: a rigid perimeter member terminating in a low-friction bearing face with a clearance remaining along at least part of it through which ambient air enters continuously, and an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric while that ingress continues. This turn's edits make that position more defensible rather than less.
